messages.subject: Repeated measure ANOVA
messages.body_plain:
Just a quick question:

How do I do a repeated measure ANOVA in R? [So far I've done this with
SPSS but I'm trying to "convert" to R ;)]

What I mean is this:

Imagine you have carried out an experiment on sentence judgments and
you get the following results:

               Condition A1a     Condition A1b     Condition A2a ...
subject 1      1.2323                2.3224                -2.5654 ...
subject 2      1.0672                1.8545                -1.7777 ...
...

It's a within-subject experiment (i.e. every subject sees all
conditions), so the scores in row 1, i.e. subject 1, are not
independent. As I said I know how to test this in SPSS, but how can I
do it in R? And how can I test for interaction effects [e.g. how do I
carry out post-hoc Tukey-test].

Thanks in advance!

Thomas Hoffmann

messages.subject: Re: Repeated measures ANOVA
messages.body_plain:
Hi

This is a recurring topic on the general R-Help list, which already indicates that it is a not-so-easy question. An example for a very simple case can be found here:
<http://cran.r-project.org/doc/contrib/Lemon-kickstart/kr_repms.html>

Another site that may be useful is this:
<http://www.ats.ucla.edu/STAT/R/seminars/Repeated_Measures/repeated_measures.htm>

However, I should like to mention that ANOVA in R is not without its traps if you don't know your way around ANOVA well. The major obstacle is that the general functions in R to do ANOVAs - aov(...) or anova(lm(...)) - use type I sums of squares whereas SPSS, Statistica, and other software by default uses a type III sums of squares approach (cf. <http://animsci.agrenv.mcgill.ca/servers/anbreed/statisticsII/type1.htm>). In a nutshell, the difference between the two is that in the former the order in which the predictors are entered into the regression equation is important whereas in the latter it is not. This is nice because you get each variable's contribution in isolation. This is bad because getting each variable in isolation is worthless in the presence of higher-order interactions ... Thus, you might wish to explore this issue together with the ANOVA issue.

Hope that helps at least a little,
STG
--
Stefan Th. Gries

http://www.linguistics.ucsb.edu/faculty/stgries
